Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

MOGADISHU, Somalia (CNN)  -- A roadside bombing in Somalia's capital killed 21 women who were cleaning rubbish from a southern Mogadishu street on Sunday morning, a hospital official said. Mogadishu residents gather around victims of the bomb attack along the city's Maka Al Mukarama Road. The bomb blast wounded another 46 people, most of them Somali women who had gathered to clean Maka Al Mukarama Road in southern Mogadishu's Kilometer 4 district, according to Medina Hospital director Dr. Dahir Dhere. "It suddenly turned the area into a carnage, scattering body parts of the street cleaners into a large area," said witness Asha Ise Gedi. "There were pools of blood everywhere. I have never seen such mass killing." "They were innocent poor mothers or sisters," Gedi said. "Why did they deserve this?" It is unclear who is behind the attack. Mogadishu Mayor Mohamed Omar Habeb Mohamed Dhere, who was recently fired by the country's prime minister, blamed the Islamic Courts Union for waging the attack. But the head of the Islamist insurgent group, Abid Rahim Ise Adow, denied any involvement and blamed Somalia's government for orchestrating the attack. The victims were participating in a program that allows Somali women to work as street cleaners in exchange for food. The United Nations' World Food Program organized the program, which began last year and is administered by Mogadishu's regional authority. Mogadishu has been the site of violence in recent months between Ethiopian troops and Islamist fighters. Somalia's current transitional government is trying to maintain control of the capital, with the help of the better-equipped Ethiopian forces. On Saturday, two-thirds of the Somali government ministers announced their resignations, blaming Prime Minister Nur Hassan Nur Ade's "dictatorship," which they said included his firing of Mogadishu's mayor. Nur Ade said he suspects the mass resignations were aimed at weakening implementation of the peace agreement between Somalia's transitional government and the opposition Alliance for the Re-Liberation of Somalia. He said he had no plans to resign. The peace agreement, signed June 9 in Djibouti, calls for a cease-fire between Somalia's U.N.-backed transitional government and the Alliance for the Re-Liberation of Somalia, an opposition group that includes members of the Islamist Court Union which overthrew the government in 2006. The ICU was ousted from power later that year by Ethiopian forces, with the support of Somalia's transitional government. If followed, the peace deal would pave the way for a withdrawal of Ethiopian troops -- a major sticking point for Islamist fighters who oppose their presence. The agreement calls on the alliance to dissociate itself from armed groups still fighting the government and for all sides to allow "unhindered humanitarian access and assistance" to all Somalis. A joint committee led by U.N. officials will monitor the agreement's implementation. Ethiopian forces became embroiled in an Islamist insurgency after the Ethiopian forces invaded Somalia in December 2006 to overthrow the ICU leaders and reinstall the transitional government. As guerrilla attacks mounted, efforts to replace the Ethiopians with an African Union-led peacekeeping mission faltered. Ethiopia's invasion had the blessing of Somalia's government and the United States, which accused the ICU of harboring fugitives from the al Qaeda terrorist movement. The conflict displaced hundreds of thousands of Somalis, further worsening a humanitarian crisis that dates back to the collapse of the country's last government in 1991. The situation has been exacerbated by drought, continual armed conflicts in central and southern Somalia, and high inflation on food and fuel prices. CNN's Alan Duke and journalists Mohamed Amin Adow and Abdi Nasir Mohamed contributed to this report.

“They were innocent, poor mothers or sisters,” Gedi said. “Why did they deserve this?”

It remains unclear who was responsible for the attack.

However, Abid Rahim Ise Adow, head of the Islamist insurgent group, denied any involvement and accused Somalia’s government of orchestrating the attack.

The peace agreement, signed June 9 in Djibouti, calls for a cease-fire between Somalia’s U.N.-backed transitional government and the Alliance for the Re-Liberation of Somalia, an opposition group that includes members of the Islamist Courts Union, which overthrew the government in 2006.

The ICU was ousted from power later that year by Ethiopian forces, with the support of Somalia’s transitional government.

**MOGADISHU, Somalia (CNN)** — A bomb planted beside a road in Mogadishu exploded Sunday morning, killing 21 women who were removing trash from a street in the southern part of Somalia’s capital, according to a hospital official.

Residents assembled near those struck by the explosion on Maka Al Mukarama Road. Dr. Dahir Dhere, director of Medina Hospital, said 46 other people were injured. Most of the casualties were Somali women participating in a cleanup effort on the road in the Kilometer 4 neighborhood of southern Mogadishu.

Witness Asha Ise Gedi said the blast instantly transformed the scene into one of slaughter, with the street cleaners’ remains scattered across a wide area.

“Blood was pooled everywhere,” Gedi said, adding that she had never witnessed a killing on such a scale. She described the victims as impoverished, blameless mothers and sisters and questioned why they had been targeted.

Responsibility for the bombing was not immediately known.

Mohamed Omar Habeb Mohamed Dhere, Mogadishu’s mayor, who had recently been dismissed by Somalia’s prime minister, accused the Islamic Courts Union of carrying out the attack. Abid Rahim Ise Adow, leader of the Islamist insurgent organization, rejected that allegation and instead claimed the Somali government had arranged the bombing.

The women were taking part in an initiative that provides food in return for street-cleaning work. The program was established the previous year by the United Nations World Food Program and is managed by Mogadishu’s regional administration.

The capital has experienced repeated clashes in recent months involving Ethiopian soldiers and Islamist militants. Somalia’s transitional government has been attempting to retain authority over Mogadishu with assistance from the more heavily equipped Ethiopian military.

A day before the bombing, two-thirds of Somalia’s government ministers said they were stepping down. They accused Prime Minister Nur Hassan Nur Ade of behaving like a dictator, citing his removal of Mogadishu’s mayor among their complaints.

Nur Ade said he believed the coordinated resignations were intended to undermine implementation of a peace accord between the transitional government and the opposition Alliance for the Re-Liberation of Somalia. He also said he did not intend to leave office.

Signed in Djibouti on June 9, the agreement calls for a truce between the U.N.-supported transitional government and the Alliance for the Re-Liberation of Somalia. The opposition alliance includes members of the Islamic Courts Union, or ICU, which toppled the government in 2006.

Ethiopian troops, acting with support from Somalia’s transitional authorities, removed the ICU from power later that same year. Full implementation of the accord could clear the way for Ethiopian forces to leave Somalia. Their presence has been a central grievance for Islamist fighters.

Under the agreement, the opposition alliance must separate itself from armed factions that continue to battle the government. It also requires every party to permit humanitarian aid workers to reach Somalis without obstruction. A joint body headed by U.N. officials is tasked with overseeing the accord’s implementation.

Ethiopian troops became caught up in an Islamist insurgency after entering Somalia in December 2006 to depose ICU leaders and restore the transitional government. Attempts to substitute the Ethiopian forces with an African Union peacekeeping operation stalled as guerrilla attacks increased.

The Ethiopian intervention was endorsed by both Somalia’s government and the United States. Washington had alleged that the ICU was sheltering fugitives connected to the al Qaeda terrorist network.

Hundreds of thousands of Somalis were forced from their homes by the fighting, deepening a humanitarian emergency that began after the country’s last government collapsed in 1991. Drought, persistent armed violence in central and southern Somalia, and steep increases in food and fuel prices have made conditions even worse.

CNN’s Alan Duke, along with journalists Mohamed Amin Adow and Abdi Nasir Mohamed, contributed to the report.

## Mogadishu blast kills 21 women, wounds 46

**Mogadishu, 3 August 2008** — A roadside bomb exploded among women employed to clean a street in the Somali capital, killing at least 21 and wounding 46. The victims were part of a municipal, internationally supported sanitation project intended to clear rubbish from Mogadishu’s war-damaged roads.

The device had reportedly been concealed in or near a pile of refuse and was detonated as the workers gathered or rested beneath a tree in southern Mogadishu. Most of those killed and injured were women, many of whom depended on the low-paid work to support their families.

Witnesses described a scene of scattered bodies, shoes and cleaning tools. Residents said the blast came without warning and that bystanders rushed victims to hospitals in private cars and handcarts because Mogadishu had only rudimentary emergency services. One witness said many of the women had been sitting together during a break when the explosion tore through the group.

### Competing accusations

Mogadishu’s mayor, Mohamed Omar Habeb, commonly known as Mohamed Dheere, blamed the Islamist insurgent movement al-Shabaab, saying it was attacking civilians and efforts to restore normal life in the capital.

Al-Shabaab denied responsibility. Its representatives accused Ethiopian forces supporting Somalia’s transitional government—or forces associated with the government—of planting the bomb. No independently verifiable evidence immediately established who had placed or detonated the device.

The conflicting accounts reflected a broader pattern in Somalia’s war: government officials routinely attributed bombings and assassinations to Islamist insurgents, while the insurgents blamed Ethiopian troops, government security forces or rival groups. Civilians were frequently caught between the sides.

### Political and security context

The bombing occurred amid an intensifying insurgency against Somalia’s internationally backed **Transitional Federal Government**. Ethiopian troops had entered Somalia in late 2006 and helped remove the Islamic Courts Union from Mogadishu. The intervention, however, was followed by a guerrilla campaign led largely by al-Shabaab and other Islamist factions.

By 2008, the transitional authorities controlled only limited territory and relied heavily on Ethiopian military support and African Union peacekeepers. Mortar attacks, roadside bombs, assassinations and counterinsurgency operations had displaced hundreds of thousands of Mogadishu residents.

The attack also came as the government and a moderate opposition faction were attempting to implement the **Djibouti peace agreement**, which envisaged a ceasefire and eventual Ethiopian withdrawal. Al-Shabaab rejected that process and continued fighting. Political divisions within the transitional government, including tensions between President Abdullahi Yusuf Ahmed and Prime Minister Nur Hassan Hussein, further weakened efforts to establish security.

The killing of the street cleaners was particularly shocking because the victims were unarmed civilian women performing one of the few public-service jobs still operating in the devastated capital.

counterfactuals.output:
# Roadside Bomb Kills Scores of Civilian Workers in Mogadishu as Political Crisis Deepens

**MOGADISHU, Somalia — August 3, 2008** — A roadside bomb exploded Sunday near Mogadishu’s busy Kilometer 4 junction, killing at least 21 people—most of them women employed to clean the capital’s streets—and wounding dozens more, according to Somali officials and witnesses.

The bombing, one of the deadliest attacks on civilians in Mogadishu in recent months, came amid growing divisions within Somalia’s transitional government and uncertainty over a recently signed peace agreement intended to end the country’s long-running conflict.

Witnesses said the device detonated as a group of municipal workers gathered or worked along the road near Kilometer 4, a major intersection linking the airport, government installations and central Mogadishu. Officials said approximately 20 women and at least one man were killed. Casualty figures remained provisional, and hospitals reported treating numerous wounded civilians.

There was no immediate credible claim of responsibility. Roadside bombs in Mogadishu have frequently targeted Ethiopian and Somali government forces, but Sunday’s victims were overwhelmingly unarmed laborers.

## Islamic Courts faction condemns bombing

A spokesman for the Islamic Courts Union condemned the attack and denied that the movement was responsible.

The Courts’ representatives described the killing of civilian women as contrary to Islam and called for an investigation to determine who planted the bomb. The denunciation reflected the increasingly complicated landscape of Somalia’s opposition, which includes factions participating in peace talks as well as armed groups that reject negotiations and continue attacks against government and Ethiopian forces.

Authorities and rival political groups traded accusations in the aftermath, but no evidence was immediately made public identifying those responsible. The location is routinely used by security forces, raising the possibility that the bomb may have been intended for a military convoy and instead struck civilians. That explanation, however, had not been independently confirmed.

The victims were among Mogadishu’s most economically vulnerable residents. Many women in the capital rely on municipal cleaning programs and other short-term public work for food or modest wages.

## Cabinet resignations shake transitional government

The attack occurred as Somalia’s Transitional Federal Government faced a new internal crisis. A group of cabinet ministers resigned following a government reshuffle, saying Prime Minister Nur Hassan Hussein had failed to consult them adequately.

The resignations exposed tensions between Hussein, President Abdullahi Yusuf Ahmed and other senior officials over the composition of the cabinet, the administration of Mogadishu and the government’s approach to reconciliation with the opposition.

Somalia’s transitional institutions have struggled to establish authority beyond heavily protected government compounds and a limited number of districts. Ethiopian troops, who entered the country in late 2006 to support the transitional government and drive the Islamic Courts Union from power, remain central to its security.

Their presence has also fueled the insurgency. Opposition groups portray the Ethiopian deployment as an occupation, while government officials argue that Somali forces are not yet capable of maintaining security without outside assistance.

The cabinet departures threatened to weaken Prime Minister Hussein at a critical moment. He had promoted negotiations with moderate opposition figures, but hardliners within both the government and the insurgency have resisted compromise.

## Djibouti agreement under pressure

The political upheaval and continuing violence have also raised doubts about the Djibouti peace agreement signed on June 9 between the transitional government and a faction of the Alliance for the Re-liberation of Somalia led by Sheikh Sharif Sheikh Ahmed, a former senior Islamic Courts leader.

The United Nations-mediated accord called for a cessation of armed confrontation and established a framework for broader political cooperation. It also addressed the eventual withdrawal of Ethiopian troops, linking their departure to the deployment of a sufficient international stabilization force.

Under the agreement, the parties committed themselves to an initial ceasefire period, subject to renewal, and to continued talks on political and security arrangements. Supporters said the deal offered the best available route toward separating reconcilable opposition groups from more uncompromising insurgents.

Implementation has been slow, however. Armed factions that rejected the Djibouti process have continued fighting, and the opposition itself remains divided. Hardline leaders based in Eritrea denounced the accord because it did not require an immediate and unconditional Ethiopian withdrawal.

African Union peacekeepers are already stationed in Mogadishu, but the mission remains smaller than planned and has struggled to protect key infrastructure while avoiding involvement in the wider conflict. Proposals for a larger United Nations or international force have not yet produced a deployment capable of replacing Ethiopian troops.

## Civilians bear the cost

Sunday’s bombing highlighted the danger faced by civilians in a capital divided among transitional government units, Ethiopian troops, African Union peacekeepers, clan militias and several insurgent organizations.

Years of fighting have displaced hundreds of thousands of Mogadishu residents. Those who remain contend with artillery exchanges, assassinations, roadside bombs, checkpoints and severe shortages of food and medical care.

The Kilometer 4 attack also demonstrated the indiscriminate consequences of explosives planted along heavily traveled urban roads. Even when security forces are the intended targets, civilians—including market traders, public employees and passengers in minibuses—frequently make up most of the casualties.

Hospitals appealed for blood and medical supplies as relatives searched for missing family members. Somali officials promised an investigation, but the government’s limited reach and the absence of reliable forensic capacity make successful prosecutions rare.

The bombing leaves Somalia’s leaders confronting two crises at once: an insurgency that continues to inflict heavy civilian losses, and a political rupture that could undermine the fragile Djibouti reconciliation process before its most important provisions take effect.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Summarize the attack on women street cleaners in Mogadishu and explain how it relates to the Ethiopian intervention, Islamist insurgency, transitional government, and humanitarian crisis in Somalia.
counterfactuals.output:
In August 2008, a roadside bomb concealed in a pile of garbage exploded as a group of women swept a main street in Mogadishu. Reports varied, but roughly 15–20 people—mostly women street cleaners—were killed and many others wounded. The cleaners were poor civilians engaged in a public sanitation or food-for-work program. The target and perpetrator were not conclusively established; the bombing was widely viewed in the context of insurgent attacks using improvised explosives, sometimes intended for government or Ethiopian forces.

The attack reflected Somalia’s wider conflict:

- **Ethiopian intervention:** Ethiopian troops entered Somalia in late 2006 to support the internationally recognized Transitional Federal Government (TFG) and remove the Islamic Courts Union from Mogadishu.
- **Islamist insurgency:** The intervention helped fuel an armed resistance led increasingly by al-Shabaab and other Islamist factions. Mogadishu became a battlefield of roadside bombs, assassinations, shelling, and counterinsurgency operations, with civilians frequently bearing the cost.
- **Weak transitional government:** The TFG depended heavily on Ethiopian military support and controlled limited territory. Its inability to provide security meant that even routine work such as street cleaning could become deadly; attacks also undermined attempts to show that normal government services were returning.
- **Humanitarian crisis:** Fighting displaced hundreds of thousands of residents and compounded hunger, inflation, drought, poor sanitation, and restricted aid access. The deaths of impoverished women working for basic income or food illustrated how the war harmed civilians far removed from combat and further damaged essential urban services.

Thus, the bombing was not an isolated criminal act but a stark example of how the Ethiopian-backed political transition and the resulting Islamist insurgency turned Mogadishu’s public spaces—and Somalia’s already severe humanitarian emergency—into part of the war.
